items.prompt: What is 'framing', as defined in L1?
choices: Choosing which true facts to emphasize, and in what order, without omitting anything material or asserting anything false
Presenting information in whatever order events actually happened
Selectively hiding negative facts to make an outcome look better
Adding persuasive but false details to strengthen a narrative
items.explanation: Framing is specifically about emphasis and order among true, complete facts — not omission (that's spin) or fabrication (that's lying).
items.reference:
Framing
✅ All facts true
✅ Nothing material omitted
Why: this is what separates legitimate narrative choice from spin or lying.

items.prompt: According to L1, does framing require changing any facts?
choices: No — the facts underneath stay identical either way
Yes — framing always requires adjusting at least one fact slightly
Yes, but only facts that are negative
L1 doesn't address whether framing changes facts
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that framing changes emphasis and order, not the underlying facts — the same set of true facts can be told multiple ways.
items.reference:
Framing
✅ All facts true
✅ Nothing material omitted
Why: this is what separates legitimate narrative choice from spin or lying.

items.prompt: What is 'emphasis', as defined in L1?
choices: How much space, prominence, or lead-position a given fact gets in a narrative
Whether a fact is stated in bold text or plain text
The total number of facts included in a narrative
Whether a fact is delivered verbally or in writing
items.explanation: Emphasis is specifically about space and prominence within a narrative — independent of formatting choices like bold text or delivery medium.
items.reference:
Emphasis
📍 Lead position vs. buried
📏 Space devoted to a fact
Why: emphasis is independent of whether a fact is positive or negative.

items.prompt: According to L1, is emphasis independent of whether a fact is positive or negative?
choices: Yes — emphasis is about prominence and space, not about the fact's sentiment
No — only positive facts can be emphasized
No — only negative facts can be emphasized
L1 doesn't address this relationship
items.explanation: L1 defines emphasis as independent of sentiment — a negative fact can be emphasized just as deliberately as a positive one.
items.reference:
Emphasis
📍 Lead position vs. buried
📏 Space devoted to a fact
Why: emphasis is independent of whether a fact is positive or negative.

items.prompt: What is 'spin', as defined in L1?
choices: Presenting true individual facts in a way that omits material context, creating a misleading overall impression
Any narrative that emphasizes positive facts over negative ones
Stating something that is factually false
Presenting facts in chronological order
items.explanation: Spin is specifically about material omission creating a misleading impression, even though every individual statement remains true — distinct from both framing and lying.
items.reference:
Spin
✅ Every sentence checks out true
🚫 Material fact missing entirely
Why: the tell is in what's missing, not in any single sentence.

items.prompt: According to L1, why is spin the 'harder case' to identify compared to lying?
choices: Every individual sentence in a spun narrative can be checked and found true — the tell isn't in any single sentence
Spin is actually impossible to detect under any circumstances
Spin only occurs in written communication, never spoken
L1 states spin and lying are equally easy to identify
items.explanation: L1 explains this exact difficulty — spin's individual sentences all check out as true, so the problem only becomes visible by checking for what's absent.
items.reference:
Spin
✅ Every sentence checks out true
🚫 Material fact missing entirely
Why: the tell is in what's missing, not in any single sentence.

items.prompt: What is 'narrative ownership', as defined in L1?
choices: Proactively telling the story of your own work yourself, rather than leaving it to be assembled secondhand
Legally claiming credit for a project's outcome regardless of who did the work
Refusing to let anyone else discuss your project
Writing a project's documentation before the project is finished
items.explanation: Narrative ownership is specifically about proactively telling your own story, rather than a legal claim or a restriction on others discussing the work.
items.reference:
Narrative ownership
🗣️ Tell it yourself, proactively
🔀 Not assembled secondhand
Why: the alternative to owning the story is someone else's version filling the gap.

items.prompt: According to L1's scenario, both team updates were written from the same three facts. Were both updates true?
choices: Yes — both updates were entirely true, with no facts added or removed
No — one update contained a false statement
No — both updates omitted the outage entirely
It's impossible to tell from L1 whether either update was true
items.explanation: L1 states explicitly that both updates were entirely true, with neither adding nor removing a single fact — the difference was purely in order and emphasis.
items.reference:
Narrative ownership
🗣️ Tell it yourself, proactively
🔀 Not assembled secondhand
Why: the alternative to owning the story is someone else's version filling the gap.

items.prompt: According to L1's scenario, by what percentage did page load time improve?
choices: 3 weeks
12 minutes
items.explanation: Page load time dropped from 3.2s to 1.9s, a 40.6% improvement — one of the three core facts in the scenario.
items.reference:
The three facts
⚡ 40.6% faster load time
⏰ 3 weeks late
🐛 12-minute outage
Why: all three facts stay identical across every version of the story.

items.prompt: According to L1's scenario, how long did the outage caused by the caching bug last?
choices: 12 minutes
12 hours
3 weeks
It's not specified in L1
items.explanation: The scenario specifies a 12-minute outage from the caching bug, which was found and fixed.
items.reference:
The three facts
⚡ 40.6% faster load time
⏰ 3 weeks late
🐛 12-minute outage
Why: all three facts stay identical across every version of the story.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what distinguishes 'spin' from 'framing'?
choices: In spin, at least one material fact is missing entirely; in framing, every material fact is present
Spin always contains at least one false statement; framing never does
Framing is always used for negative facts; spin is always used for positive ones
There is no real distinction — L2 treats them as the same thing
items.explanation: L2's table draws this exact line — both framing and spin keep every stated fact true, but spin omits material facts entirely while framing includes all of them.
items.reference:
The three-way table
Framing: true + complete
Spin: true + incomplete
Lying: false
Why: two independent questions, not one vague judgment call.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what's true of every stated fact in a lying narrative, compared to spin or framing?
choices: At least one stated fact is false — this is the one category where the 'every fact true?' answer is 'no'
Every fact is true, exactly like framing and spin
Lying always contains more facts than framing or spin
L2's table doesn't address the truth value of facts in lying
items.explanation: L2's table marks lying as the only category where 'every stated fact true?' is answered 'no' — framing and spin both keep every individual statement true.
items.reference:
The three-way table
Framing: true + complete
Spin: true + incomplete
Lying: false
Why: two independent questions, not one vague judgment call.

items.prompt: According to L2, what is the test for whether an omitted fact makes a narrative spin?
choices: Whether a reasonable reader's understanding of the outcome would actually change if they learned the fact
Whether the fact was mentioned in any prior conversation
Whether the fact is longer than one sentence to explain
Whether the fact happened before or after the project's official end date
items.explanation: L2 defines materiality specifically as whether a reasonable reader's understanding would change — not sentence length, timing, or prior mentions.
items.reference:
Materiality
❓ Would the reader's understanding change?
Why: not "everything" — just what actually changes the picture.

items.prompt: According to L2, does an honest narrative have to include literally every detail about a project?
choices: No — the test is materiality, not completeness of every possible detail
Yes — omitting any detail at all, no matter how minor, counts as spin
Yes, but only for projects that involve an outage
L2 doesn't address whether every detail must be included
items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects an 'everything' standard in favor of materiality — a detail like which IDE was used can reasonably be skipped without it being spin.
items.reference:
Materiality
❓ Would the reader's understanding change?
Why: not "everything" — just what actually changes the picture.

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, what's the first question to ask before sending a narrative out?
choices: Is every stated fact actually true?
Is the narrative shorter than 100 words?
Has a manager already approved the narrative?
Does the narrative mention every team member by name?
items.explanation: L2's flowchart starts with checking factual truth — if that fails, the process stops there, since a false statement is lying regardless of what else is true.
items.reference:
The self-check flowchart
1. All facts true?
2. Any material fact missing?
Why: two independent checks, usable in the moment, not after the fact.

items.prompt: According to L2, if every fact is true and no material fact is missing, what does the flowchart conclude?
choices: This is legitimate framing — emphasis and order are the author's to choose
This still needs a third check before it can be considered honest
This is automatically classified as spin regardless of the other answers
The flowchart has no conclusion for this specific combination
items.explanation: L2's flowchart concludes with legitimate framing once both checks pass — true facts, nothing material missing — with emphasis and order left entirely to the author's judgment.
items.reference:
The self-check flowchart
1. All facts true?
2. Any material fact missing?
Why: two independent checks, usable in the moment, not after the fact.

items.prompt: According to L2, is reporting facts in strict chronological order a 'neutral' way to avoid the risks of framing?
choices: No — chronological order isn't neutral either; it just means someone else's instinctive reaction becomes the default framing
Yes — chronological order is the only truly neutral way to present facts
Yes, but only for updates shorter than one paragraph
L2 doesn't address whether chronological order is neutral
items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects the idea that chronological order is neutral — not choosing a deliberate framing just hands the framing decision to instinct or convention instead.
items.reference:
Why avoiding framing doesn't work
🎲 No deliberate order ≠ neutral
📖 The reader's assumptions fill the gap
Why: owning the narrative honestly is the alternative to an undeliberate default, not a departure from honesty.

items.prompt: According to L2, what fills the gap when a narrative isn't deliberately framed?
choices: The reader's own assumptions, which fill in whatever wasn't deliberately shaped
A legal requirement to disclose every fact equally
Nothing — an undeliberate narrative has no effect on how it's read
The most senior person in the room automatically reframes it
items.explanation: L2 states that without deliberate framing, the reader's own assumptions (like 'no news is good news,' or its opposite) end up doing the framing instead.
items.reference:
Why avoiding framing doesn't work
🎲 No deliberate order ≠ neutral
📖 The reader's assumptions fill the gap
Why: owning the narrative honestly is the alternative to an undeliberate default, not a departure from honesty.

No — Draft A contains a false statement about the outage
No — Draft A omits the page-load improvement entirely
L3 doesn't evaluate Draft A against L2's check
items.explanation: L3 explicitly states Draft A passes the honesty check — the issue with it is undeliberate emphasis, not dishonesty.
items.reference:
Draft A: buried lead
✅ Passes the honesty check
😬 Setback leads, result is compressed
Why: undeliberate framing, not dishonest framing.

It uses more words overall than Draft B
It was written faster than the other two drafts
It was sent to a different audience than the other drafts

items.reference:

😬 Setback leads, result is compressed

items.prompt: According to L3, does a reader of Draft B (honest framing) end up with more or less concrete information than a reader of Draft A?
choices: More — Draft B names the specific cause and duration of the outage, rather than vaguely gesturing at 'issues'
Less — Draft B deliberately omits some details to stay concise
The exact same amount, just in a different order
L3 doesn't compare the two drafts' level of detail
items.explanation: L3 states Draft B's reader ends up with more concrete information than Draft A's — the outage cause and duration are named specifically, not vaguely referenced.
items.reference:
Draft B: honest framing
🎯 Result leads, with real numbers
📋 Setback named specifically, not vaguely
Why: more concrete detail than Draft A, just organized deliberately.

items.prompt: According to L3, what changed between Draft A and Draft B, given both pass the same honesty check?
choices: Deliberate emphasis — the result leads with real numbers, and the setback is named with specific detail instead of vague language
Draft B added new facts that weren't in Draft A
Draft B removed the outage from the narrative entirely
Nothing meaningful changed between the two drafts
items.explanation: L3 attributes the difference entirely to deliberate emphasis and specificity, not to any change in which facts are present.
items.reference:
Draft B: honest framing
🎯 Result leads, with real numbers
📋 Setback named specifically, not vaguely
Why: more concrete detail than Draft A, just organized deliberately.

items.prompt: According to L3, what specifically makes Draft C spin rather than framing?
choices: The outage — a material fact — is omitted entirely, not de-emphasized or summarized
Draft C contains a factual error about the page load improvement
Draft C is written in a different tone than the other two drafts
Draft C is significantly longer than Draft A or B
items.explanation: L3 identifies the outage's complete omission — not de-emphasis, but absence — as exactly what crosses the line from framing into spin.
items.reference:
Draft C: spin
✅ Every sentence is true
🚫 Outage omitted entirely
Why: the tell L2 predicted — no false sentence, but a misleading overall impression.

No — the page load statistic in Draft C is inaccurate

L3 doesn't evaluate whether Draft C's sentences are individually true
